title: 2  Setting Up Your Environment
text:
Install JASP (nightly build)
You need a recent version of JASP to develop modules. Nightly builds include the latest features.

Windows & macOSLinux


Download the latest nightly build for your platform.


# 1. Install flatpak if needed: https://flatpak.org/setup/
# 2. Add the beta repository
flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub-beta https://flathub.org/beta-repo/flathub-beta.flatpakrepo

# 3. Install JASP beta
flatpak install flathub-beta org.jaspstats.JASP

# 4. Launch in development mode
flatpak run --branch=beta --devel org.jaspstats.JASP






Warning



JASP remembers the branch it was launched from. To switch back to stable: flatpak run --branch=stable org.jaspstats.JASP


If you see runtime/org.kde.Sdk/x86_64/6.7 not installed, fix it with:
flatpak install org.kde.Sdk   # choose version 6.7

title: 2  Setting Up Your Environment
text:
Install and configure Git
Git is a version control system that tracks changes to your code over time. It lets you undo mistakes, work on different features in parallel (via branches), and collaborate with others through platforms like GitHub. All JASP modules are hosted on GitHub, so you’ll need Git throughout your development workflow.

Install Git

macOSWindowsLinux


Git comes with the Xcode Command Line Tools. Open a terminal and run:
git --version
If Git isn’t installed, macOS will prompt you to install the tools. Alternatively, install via Homebrew: brew install git.


Download and install from git-scm.com/downloads. The default settings are fine. This also installs Git Bash, a terminal you can use for Git commands.


# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install git

# Fedora
sudo dnf install git





Configure your identity
Git tags every commit with your name and email. Set these once:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.org"


Create a GitHub account
If you don’t have one yet, sign up at github.com. JASP modules live under the jasp-stats organisation.


Key Git concepts
You don’t need to be a Git expert to develop JASP modules, but a few concepts come up constantly:







Concept
What it means




Repository (repo)
A project folder tracked by Git


Clone
Download a copy of a remote repository to your computer


Fork
Create your own copy of someone else’s repository on GitHub


Commit
Save a snapshot of your changes


Branch
A parallel line of development (e.g., feature/my-analysis)


Push / Pull
Upload your commits to GitHub / download others’ commits


Pull request (PR)
Ask the maintainers to merge your branch into the main project





Learning resources

GitHub in 20 Minutes — beginner-friendly video introduction to GitHub
Git in 15 Minutes — beginner-friendly video introduction to Git
Git User Manual — the official comprehensive reference
Pro Git book — free online book, excellent for beginners and advanced users
GitHub Skills — interactive tutorials for learning Git with GitHub
Oh My Git! — a game to learn Git visually

For more R packaging, QML, and JASP-specific resources, see the Resources appendix.
For the JASP-specific Git workflow (forking, branching, pull requests), see the Git Workflow chapter. That chapter builds on the basics covered here and explains the day-to-day workflow you’ll use when contributing to JASP modules. The Publishing Your Module chapter covers how to submit your module to the JASP Module Library.

title: 2  Setting Up Your Environment
section: Fork and clone the module template
text:
Fork and clone the module template

Go to jaspModuleTemplate and click Fork.
Clone your fork:

git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/jaspModuleTemplate.git
cd jaspModuleTemplate
Alternatively, fork an existing module from jasp-stats.

title: 2  Setting Up Your Environment
text:
Package Management with renv
JASP modules use renv to lock package versions. This ensures that your module builds reproducibly and that collaborators (and CI) use the exact same dependency versions.
Every module repository should contain a renv.lock file. When you start working on a module, bootstrap the renv environment with this script:
# Set your GitHub PAT to avoid rate limits during package installation
Sys.setenv(GITHUB_PAT = "<your PAT>")

# Activate the renv project (or confirm it's already active)
if (is.null(renv::project())) {
  message("This isn't an active renv project.")
  renv::activate()
} else {
  message("We're in an active renv project.")
}

# Install all locked dependencies
message("Restoring/synchronizing the project library.")
renv::restore()

# Install the module itself into the renv library
message("Installing the package.")
renv::install(".")

# Print the library path — you'll need this for JASP developer mode
message("R libPath for developer mode:\n", .libPaths()[1])
The last line prints the library path for your newly installed module. Copy this path — you will paste it into JASP’s developer mode settings (see below).






Tip



When you add or update a dependency, run renv::snapshot() to update the lockfile and commit it.

title: 2  Setting Up Your Environment
section: Install your module as an R package
text:
Install your module as an R package
With renv active, the simplest way is:
renv::install(".")
Alternatively, from the terminal:
R CMD INSTALL . --preclean --no-multiarch --with-keep.source
Note the library path where the module is installed — you’ll need it for developer mode. Run .libPaths()[1] in R to see it.

title: 2  Setting Up Your Environment
text:
Configure JASP for development

Recommended: renv mode

Open JASP
Menu (☰) → Preferences → Advanced
Check Developer mode
Check Enable renv mode
Set the libpath where you installed the module
Enter the module name (as listed in DESCRIPTION)




Developer module setup with renv



Go back to the main JASP window
Click the + icon (top-right) → Install Developer Module




Installing the developer module

title: 2  Setting Up Your Environment
text:
GitHub Personal Access Token
If module installation fails with rate-limiting errors:



Installation failure due to GitHub rate limiting


Create a GitHub Personal Access Token (no special permissions needed — it just identifies you as a legitimate user).
In JASP: Preferences → Advanced → uncheck Use default PAT for Github → paste your token → press Enter/Tab.

title: 2  Setting Up Your Environment
text:
The development cycle




graph LR
  A[Edit R/QML files] --> B[Recompile module]
  B --> C[Refresh in JASP]
  C --> D[Test changes]
  D --> A






Edit your R and/or QML files in your editor of choice
Recompile: R CMD INSTALL . --preclean --no-multiarch --with-keep.source
Refresh: in JASP, click + → find your module → click the blue refresh button (🔄)

You must recompile to see changes — JASP loads from the installed package in the renv library.






Tip



Start with the QML interface before writing the R analysis. This lets you iterate on the UI quickly and see option names before writing the backend code.

title: 14  Versioning & Releases
text:
14.1 Version Numbers
Module versions follow a three-part scheme: major.minor.patch (e.g., 0.19.1). The version is defined in two places and must match:



File
Location




DESCRIPTION
Version: 0.19.1


inst/Description.qml
version: "0.19.1"



For routine pull requests, the patch component is now handled automatically: when a PR is merged, the z in x.y.z is incremented for you. In practice, that means you mainly need to think about the minor version.

title: 14  Versioning & Releases
text:
14.2 When to Bump




flowchart TD
    A[Module under development] --> B{Significant new feature\nor planned release?}
    B -- No --> C[Open PRs and merge them]
    C --> D[Patch bump happens automatically]
    D --> A
    B -- Yes --> E[Manually bump minor version]
    E --> F[Continue development and testing]
    F --> G{Ready for release?}
    G -- No --> A
    G -- Yes --> H[Ask a core programmer to make the official release]
    H --> A





Rule: let merged PRs handle ordinary patch bumps, but manually bump the minor version whenever you introduce a meaningful new feature or want to mark a new release cycle.
This keeps the versioning workflow predictable:

Small fixes do not require manual patch bookkeeping.
Feature work still gets a clear version step when users should notice a change.
Releases remain easy to track in both the module library and the changelog.


14.2.1 How high to bump
In day-to-day work, there are now two common cases:

Small bug fix merged via PR: 0.19.1 → 0.19.2 automatically
New feature or new release cycle: bump 0.19.1 → 0.20.0 manually before or alongside the feature/release work
Major rework: 0.19.1 → 1.0.0 if you intentionally want a major release

You may also align with the current JASP release number (e.g., bump to 0.96 when JASP 0.96 ships), but this is optional.

title: 14  Versioning & Releases
text:
14.3 NEWS.md
Every module now includes a NEWS.md file. Treat this as the standard changelog for user-facing changes, bug fixes, and new features.

Update NEWS.md alongside your code.
PR automation checks whether NEWS.md changed and reminds you if it did not.
While work is still ongoing, add entries under Development.
When you are preparing an actual release, move those items under the new version heading.

If you are unsure where to place a small fix, the default is simple: put it under Development until you are ready to cut a release.

title: 14  Versioning & Releases
text:
14.4 Release Workflow for Official Modules
Official modules live under jasp-stats/ on GitHub.

Development: open and merge PRs as usual. After merge, the patch version in DESCRIPTION is raised automatically.
Beta testing: if changes are detected, beta builds of official modules are generated once per day and can be installed from JASP’s module library.
Changelog: keep NEWS.md updated during development so release notes are ready when needed.
Release: when the module is ready for an official release, contact a core programmer to create it.

title: 14  Versioning & Releases
text:
14.5 Release Workflow for Community Modules
Community modules live under your personal GitHub account.

Development: push to your own repository.
Submission: register your module in the community registry (see Chapter 15).
Updates: open cross-fork PRs to the jasp-stats-modules fork of your repo.
Beta/Release: after merge, automated systems build and publish a beta release.

title: 14  Versioning & Releases
text:
14.6 Upgrades.qml and Versions
Upgrade entries in Upgrades.qml reference module versions, not JASP versions. When you bump a version and rename or remove options, add an upgrade block targeting that version range (see Chapter 13).

title: 15  Publishing Your Module
text:
15.1 Community Module Submission
Community modules are managed through the modules-registry repository on GitHub under the jasp-stats-modules organization. To add your module, choose one of the two options below.

15.1.1 Option 1: Contact the Team
Open an issue on the JASP issue tracker or send a message on Mattermost. The JASP team will add it for you.


15.1.2 Option 2: Pull Request

Fork the modules-registry repository.
Add a new .yaml file in the modules-metadata/ folder. The filename should match your module name (e.g., jaspMyModule.yaml). The file needs two fields:
name: "jaspMyModule"
gitUrl: "https://github.com/yourname/jaspMyModule"
Create a pull request to the modules-registry repository.
After review and a successful merge, the JASP organization will fork your module repository and it will appear in the community modules list. Users running the JASP beta or nightly can then install it.

title: 15  Publishing Your Module
text:
15.2 Updating a Community Module
Once your module is in the registry, the JASP organization maintains a fork of your repository at https://github.com/jasp-stats-modules/YourModuleName. When you have new features or bug fixes ready, open a cross-fork pull request from your repository to this fork:

Find the fork: https://github.com/jasp-stats-modules/YourModuleName
Create cross-fork PR:

Go to the JASP fork → Pull Requests → New Pull Request
Click “compare across forks”
Set:

Base repository: jasp-stats-modules/YourModuleName (JASP’s fork)
Base branch: master or main
Head repository: yourname/YourModuleName (your repo)
Compare branch: your update branch

Click Create pull request

Review: the JASP team reviews and may request adjustments.
Merge & sync: once merged, automated systems build and publish a beta release.

title: 15  Publishing Your Module
text:
15.3 Updating an Official Module
Official modules (jasp-stats/jasp*) sync automatically:

After a PR is merged, the patch version in DESCRIPTION is bumped automatically.
Bump the minor version yourself when you add a substantial feature or want to start a new release cycle.
Beta builds are generated once per day when changes are detected.
Keep NEWS.md updated as you work; use a Development heading until you are ready to cut a release.
For a proper official release, ask a core programmer.

title: 15  Publishing Your Module
text:
15.4 Module Quality Checklists

15.4.1 Official JASP Module Checklist






Important



All items should be completed before requesting an official release.



Unit tests with ≥ 70% analysis coverage
Auto-generated tests from .jasp example files (makeTestsFromExamples())
All tests pass in GitHub Actions CI (Section 10.6)
Complete help files for every analysis (inst/help/)
info properties on all QML elements for inline documentation
Informative README with module description (Section 15.5)
NEWS / changelog file maintained and updated before each release
Option names follow naming conventions (Section 8.3)
Upgrades.qml entries for any renamed/removed options (Chapter 13)
All user-visible strings wrapped for translation (Chapter 12)
Correct license headers on all source files (Chapter 17)
R style compliance (Section 8.1)
QML style compliance (Section 8.2)
Standardised error messages (Section 5.5)



15.4.2 Community JASP Module Checklist






Note



These are the minimum requirements for a community module to be accepted into the registry.



At least one test per analysis that runs without error
README with module description and usage instructions (Section 15.5)
Working example .jasp files (in tests/testthat/jaspfiles/ or examples/)
Module installs and loads without errors in current JASP nightly
Valid DESCRIPTION file with correct metadata (title, author, version, dependencies)
Valid NAMESPACE file (auto-generated or correct exports)
Description.qml with proper module name, description, version, and analysis entries



15.4.3 Optional but Recommended (Community)

Help files or info properties on QML elements
Translation-ready strings
GitHub Actions CI workflow
Upgrades.qml for backward compatibility

title: 15  Publishing Your Module
text:
15.5 Module README
Your module’s README.md is the landing page for anyone wanting to learn more about your module — we link to it from the JASP module library. A good README makes it easy to see at a glance what the module does, who maintains it, and whether the tests are passing. See jaspMetaAnalysis for a full example.
A module README should include the following:

15.5.1 Badges and maintainer
At the top, add badges for the unit test and coverage workflows, plus the maintainer name(s). Replace jaspMyModule and the maintainer details as appropriate:
<div align="right">

[![Unit Tests](https://github.com/jasp-stats/jaspMyModule/actions/workflows/unittests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jasp-stats/jaspMyModule/actions/workflows/unittests.yml)
[![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/jasp-stats/jaspMyModule/branch/master/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/jasp-stats/jaspMyModule)
<br>
<b>Maintainer:</b> <a href="https://github.com/username/">Maintainer Name</a>

</div>
The codecov badge requires the coverage workflow to be set up first — see ?sec-coverage for instructions.
If multiple people share maintainer duties (e.g., one for frequentist and one for Bayesian analyses):
<b>Maintainers:</b> <a href="https://github.com/JohnnyDoorn/">Johnny van Doorn (Freq)</a><br>
 <a href="https://github.com/vandenman/">Don van den Bergh (Bayes)</a>


15.5.2 Module description
Add a short overview of what your module does: which analyses it provides, and what kind of research questions it helps answer. You can include the module icon for visual identity:
# The Meta-Analysis Module

## Overview

<img src='inst/icons/meta-analysis.svg' width='149' height='173' align='right'/>

**JASP Meta-Analysis module** is an add-on module for JASP that provides
tools for ...


15.5.3 Key R packages
List the main R packages that power your module’s analyses. This helps users and contributors understand what’s under the hood:
## R Packages

<img src='https://www.r-project.org/logo/Rlogo.svg' width='100' height='78' align='right'/>

The functionality is served by several R packages

- **metafor** — Meta-analysis ([metafor on CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=metafor))
- **metaBMA** — Bayesian model averaging for meta-analysis ([metaBMA on CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=metaBMA))
Focus on the packages that are specific to your module’s analyses — no need to list general dependencies like ggplot2 or jaspBase unless they play a central role.
